source.title: Reducing Per-Sample Interference in Stochastic Optimization

record.file_problem: None; the supplied text contains the paper and appendices.
record.tranche_reason: The paper reports image-classification test accuracy after adding a per-sample interference reduction method to standard optimizers. This bears on generalization performance, but does not directly test any of V1–V8.
record.gate_note: The paper also measures per-sample interference reduction and reports solver, approximation, runtime, and memory results. Those outcomes do not measure a claim version, so they are not included as rows. The accuracy rows below report the paper’s own comparison of its method with baseline training.
record.test_reason: Table 1 varies batch size and measures held-out classification accuracy. Appendix E explicitly holds epochs constant and scales learning rate by the square root of batch size. These results directly test V5, despite the paper's main focus on its proposed optimizer modification.
record.authors_conclusion: The record accurately paraphrases the authors' overall conclusion: their surrogate update reduces per-sample interference and generally improves classification accuracy with modest runtime overhead. Improvements are not universal, and Section 5.2 reports exceptions.
record.recipe_differences: Adds a per-sample interference reduction update procedure to SGD with momentum or AdamW, using a last-linear-layer surrogate; compares against standard training.
record.method_sensitivity: The reported accuracy effect varies with dataset, batch size, architecture, augmentation, normalization, training duration, and trust-region radius. ResNet-44 on CIFAR-10 at batch size 1024 declines; the authors attribute this to a rank-deficient, ill-conditioned Gram matrix.

fits_no_version.finding: Within a fixed batch size, the proposed interference-reducing update usually improves accuracy, with exceptions including ResNet-44 on CIFAR-10 at batch size 1024 and ResNet-50 with BatchNorm on Tiny-ImageNet.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Reducing per-sample update interference can improve classification accuracy, with gains depending on architecture, batch size, normalization, augmentation, training duration, and trust-region radius.

record.peer_reviewed: Proceedings of the 43rd International Conference on Machine Learning, PMLR 306, 2026
record.problems: For CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100, and Tiny-ImageNet, results are averaged over 5 seeds, but variation estimates are not supplied. ImageNet-100 uses a single seed. Table 1 text is flattened and the supplied rendering does not clearly preserve all table group headings; the final CIFAR-100 ViT rows therefore cannot be confidently reconstructed. The paper explicitly reports a performance drop for ResNet-44 on CIFAR-10 at batch size 1024.
record.rows_left_out: Table 1 is included where the supplied table layout permits the BASE/OURS values to be assigned. I did not reconstruct the remaining ViT-c CIFAR-100 Table 1 cells because the flattened table text does not securely associate those values with their headers. Table 2 and Table 5 accuracy results are omitted from rows because the paper's claims there concern its own intervention and trust-region hyperparameter, outside V1–V8; the overall related finding is summarized under fits_no_version.

untested.parts: Random-label fitting, natural-label generalization under the same recipe, and chance-level held-out performance with random labels.
Width sweeps beyond the width needed for zero training error.
Matched convolutional versus fully connected classifiers and the role of local connectivity.
Adaptive optimizers versus SGD on matched architectures under specified tuning budgets; optimizer choice here is confounded with architecture.

Language models; longer-training recovery of a measured small-batch versus large-batch penalty; controlled comparisons isolating learning-rate scaling, warmup, normalization, or regularization as remedies. The batch sweep already uses square-root learning-rate scaling.
Controlled dropout comparisons, training-set-size dependence, and joint dropout/weight-decay removal.
Magnitude-aware weight-perturbation sharpness and its correlation with generalization gaps. Gradient Gram matrices and their condition numbers are different measures.
Identification and removal of memorized training examples followed by retraining.

missing.what: Add the actual ViT-c CIFAR-10 batch sweep. At batch sizes 128, 256, 512, and 1024, baseline accuracies are 89.94, 89.62, 89.59, and 88.91%; modified-method accuracies are 90.34, 89.96, 90.17, and 89.61%. Compare each recipe across batch sizes using its own batch-size-128 reference.
missing.locator: Table 1; Appendix E for fixed epochs and square-root learning-rate scaling.

record.verdict_notes: The reader overlooked the fixed-epoch batch-size experiment and misassigned interleaved table columns. All reported CIFAR results average five seeds without variation estimates, so the verdicts describe numerical trends rather than established statistical significance. Table 1 reports a 0.28-point ResNet CIFAR-100 gain at batch size 128, whereas the accompanying prose says 0.25; the table values are retained. This study is not an original source for V5.

versions.untested_parts: Random-label memorization and natural-label generalization coexistence; random-label test performance.
Width sweeps beyond interpolation and test error as width increases.
Convolutional versus fully connected image classifiers and the role of local connectivity.
Matched generalization comparisons between adaptive optimizers and SGD under tuning regimes; the paper compares its added method with baselines, not optimizer families as the claim describes.
Whether large batches worsen the train–test gap under fixed epoch budgets, and the listed recipe adaptations.
Dropout versus no dropout, its dependence on training-set size, and interactions with augmentation and weight decay.
Magnitude-aware sharpness and its relationship to train–test gaps.
Removing memorized examples and measuring the resulting test accuracy.
